# Spencer J. Fox

I’m an Assistant Professor in the [School of Informatics, Computing, and Cyber Systems](https://in.nau.edu/school-informatics-computing-cyber-systems/) at Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff, Arizona.

I’m an epidemiologist, modeler, and data scientist interested in making outbreak forecasts more useful for the people who have to make decisions with them.

## The Short Version

I build and evaluate infectious disease models, usually with public health questions close at hand. A lot of my work focuses on respiratory viruses, outbreak forecasting, collaborative forecast hubs, and the strange things models do when epidemics begin to turn.

I’m especially drawn to projects that sit somewhere between a methodological puzzle and a real decision: enough statistical texture to be interesting, but grounded enough that someone might actually use the answer.

::: {.profile-note}
The recurring question behind much of my work is simple: how can we make a forecast more honest, more reliable, and more actionable without pretending that the future is less uncertain than it is?
:::

## Questions I Keep Coming Back To

::: {.profile-grid}
::: {.profile-card}
### When Do Models Fail?

Forecast errors are often most consequential near epidemic peaks and turning points. I’m interested in recognizing those failure modes and building practical ways to correct them.
:::

::: {.profile-card}
### What Makes An Ensemble Work?

More models are not automatically better. I study how forecast hubs, baselines, model selection, and ensemble design affect the predictions we ultimately communicate.
:::

::: {.profile-card}
### How Should Forecasts Travel?

A model built for one disease, country, or surveillance system should not be assumed to work everywhere. International collaborations make those assumptions visible—and make the science better.
:::
:::

## How I Like To Work

I like collaborative projects where people can think out loud, challenge the model, and be honest about what the data can support. Good science usually involves a mixture of careful planning, exploratory detours, clear writing, and somebody asking the inconvenient question at exactly the right time.

As a mentor, I want people to develop their own scientific taste: not only the ability to run an analysis, but the judgment to decide which question is worth asking, which result is believable, and how to explain it to another human.

## Away From The Computer

Outside the lab, I’m happiest hiking, backpacking, birding, camping, or skiing. Moving to Flagstaff has made it especially easy to turn “I should go outside for an hour” into a much longer adventure.

## A Few Places To Start

::: {.profile-grid}
::: {.profile-card}
### Epimodulation

A method for augmenting empirical forecasts with epidemic dynamics, especially when models have trouble anticipating peaks.

[Read the project story](../../blog/2025-11-12-epimodulation/)
:::

::: {.profile-card}
### Forecast Ensembles

Work on how many models are needed to build robust collaborative outbreak forecasts—and when smaller ensembles can do surprisingly well.

[Read the project story](../../blog/2024-10-28-ensemble-size/)
:::

::: {.profile-card}

## Want To Talk?

I’m always happy to hear about an interesting modeling question, a possible collaboration, or someone considering joining the lab. The best starting point is a short email explaining what you are thinking about and why it might overlap with our work.
